description: Second Impact Syndrome is the brain injury that can result when an athlete returns to play too soon after a hit to the head. When schools may be liable.
shortAnswer: Second Impact Syndrome (SIS) refers to the brain injury that can result when an athlete is allowed to return to his/her sport too soon after getting hit in the head, and then suffers a second impact/concussion. Trainers and coaches have a duty to protect children from SIS, and sometimes they let children return to the field too early.

faq.q: Are children at greater risk for Second Impact Syndrome?
faq.a: The medical literature suggest that younger, less developed, brains are at greater risk for Second Impact Syndrome. There have been numerous reports of young players who have suffered back-to-back head injuries and died from increased intra-cranial pressure.

faq.q: How long should a child sit out after a concussion?
faq.a: A player who suffers even a mild concussion should be benched. Most guidelines say that player should remain out of their sport for seven days after all their symptoms disappear.

faq.q: When is a school liable if my child suffers Second Impact Syndrome?
faq.a: The school district (or owner of your child's private school or college) may be liable if it failed to use reasonable policies and procedures for head injury management, did not provide its trainers/coaches with proper training, or did not require a "return to play" note from a doctor following a concussion.
